newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Lufthansa Q1 data up but Germany lags.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lufthansa Q1 data up but Germany lags.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Lufthansa AG, reporting strong growth in global passenger levels, said on Monday its first quarter results would be above year-ago levels but that it had lost passengers on its key domestic routes.

Lufthansa said the higher number of passengers on its planes, which included a 3.3 percent year-on-year rise in its passenger load factor, was particularly marked by growth in traffic to North and South America as well as to Asia.

But the airline said "fierce competition" within Germany led to a drop of almost nine percent in passenger levels within Germany in the quarter and ahead of the full liberalisation of European skies on April 1, which now allows any airline to fly anywhere within the region at any cost.

Lufthansa also reported a two percent drop to 7.17 million in the number of passengers carried aboard its planes within Europe when including Germany but a 3.8 percent rise on flights to European destinations outside of its home market.

The airline said its better first-quarter performance was due to 18.5 percent increase in the number of passengers flown between Germany and North and South America to 991,000 and a 12 percent increase to 1.01 million passengers on flights to and from Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

But the gains could not make up for a 1.2 percent overall drop in the number of passengers flown to 7.21 million in the first quarter despite the passenger load factor, or percentage of seats filled, rose 4.1 percentage points to 68.4 percent.

Lufthansa said it would release its quarterly results on May 7. The airline last year reported a 5.8 percent rise in first quarter sales but a loss from ordinary activities of 49 million marks, a 10 percent improvement over the 1995 loss.

Lufthansa faces a tough battle within Germany from upstart competitors and also from mainstays such as Deutsche BA, a unit of British Airways Plc, Air France and KLM that offer cheap tickets to lure passengers to their domestic hubs and away from Lufthansa's main hub in Frankfurt.

Lufthansa has also been aggravated by rivals cutting costs for inner-German flights, prompting the German cartel office this year to order the airline to cut airfares on its monopoly Frankfurt-Berlin route to stop subsidising competitive routes.
The airline is considering whether to spin off its domestic operations into a separate subsidiary or to give some domestic routes to its Condor charter service in a bid to lower costs.
Lufthansa also said in the report it rejected allegations by Germany's Capital magazine that it "window-dressed" accounts to make its business position appear better than reality.

The airline said last Thursday its operating profit in 1996 was just below its pre-tax profit figure of almost 700 million marks but that its 1996 results would not match those in 1995, in part due to higher fuel charges in the second half of 1996.

In addition, Lufthansa said capacity utilisation in its cargo business was slightly below the 1996 first quarter levels but that earnings per kilometre for cargo deliveries also improved in the first quarter, reversing the trend in 1996.
The airline also said average yields per available seat kilometre were again up in March over year-ago levels.
